title: What other techniques help with data skew: isolate hot keys and broadcast them separately, increase parallelism, pre-aggregate before join, use a different join strategy, or redesign the data model?
shortTitle: Other techniques that help with data skew
keyPoints: Isolate-and-broadcast removes hot keys from the shuffle path by joining them separately with a broadcast join.
Increasing shuffle parallelism helps when many moderately-hot keys collide but does not fix a single mega-key.
Pre-aggregation at the map side reduces data volume on the hot key before it crosses the shuffle boundary.
Switching to a broadcast hash join avoids shuffling the large skewed side entirely when the small side fits in memory.
Redesigning the data model by splitting a hot key into sub-keys is the most durable fix but the most expensive to implement.
In production you usually combine two or three techniques and pick based on the specific symptom.
Always start with the cheapest and most surgical technique that fits the symptom before escalating.

s1_definition.oneliner: Fight skew by isolating-and-broadcasting hot keys, increasing parallelism, pre-aggregating before the shuffle, changing the join strategy, or redesigning the model so the hot key disappears.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Isolate-and-broadcast** – Filter out the few hot keys, join them with a broadcast of the small-side rows, and union with the normal cold-key join.
- **Increase parallelism** – Raise `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` so hashing spreads moderately-hot keys across more buckets, reducing collisions.
- **Pre-aggregation** – Aggregate on the map side before the shuffle so each partition sends one partial result per key instead of millions of raw rows.
- **Different join strategy** – Use a broadcast hash join when the small side fits in memory to avoid shuffling the large skewed side entirely.
- **Data model redesign** – Split a structurally hot key into sub-keys at the source so no single key dominates, which is the most durable fix.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India one giant pooling account overwhelms a single clerk. You can pull that one account aside and handle it specially (isolate and broadcast), hire more clerks so the pile is cut into more sub-piles (increase parallelism), have each branch total its own slips before sending them in (pre-aggregate), route the work so the clerk never touches the big ledger (different join strategy), or restructure the books so the one giant account becomes many smaller sub-accounts (redesign the data model).

sections.s6_takeaway:
Beyond salting and Adaptive Query Execution, there is a toolbox of skew techniques and you pick based on the symptom. Isolate-and-broadcast removes hot keys from the shuffle path by joining them separately with a broadcast join, which works well when the hot keys are few and known. Increasing parallelism spreads moderately-hot key collisions across more partitions but cannot fix a single mega-key. Pre-aggregation shrinks the hot partition at the source by sending partial results instead of raw rows. A broadcast hash join sidesteps skew entirely when the small side fits in memory.

The deepest fix is redesigning the data model so the hot key no longer exists, for example splitting a pooling account into numbered sub-accounts. This is the most durable solution but the most expensive to implement, so you reach for it when the same hot key keeps causing incidents across many jobs rather than patching each job.

At the National Bank of India these were real decisions. A transactions join skewed on one corporate pooling account was cleanest with isolate-and-broadcast. A merchant job with dozens of colliding keys was fixed by raising shuffle partitions. A per-account counting job was fixed by pre-aggregating before the join. The rule is to start with the cheapest technique that fits the symptom, combine two or three when needed, and reserve model redesign for structural recurring problems.

Remember one sentence: start with the cheapest and most surgical skew technique that fits the symptom, combine techniques when needed, and reserve data model redesign for hot keys that keep causing incidents across many jobs.
